932.title: A resignation (2013)
932.hook: Benedict XVI announces, in Latin, that he will step down as pope
932.howItsDone: When a pope dies or resigns, the see of Rome is vacant until the cardinals meet in conclave to elect a successor; Catholics pray for the Church and for the cardinals during that time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict the Sixteenth and his first letter, Deus caritas est. Your line was God is love. What did your quiet act of charity cost you? Day nine hundred thirty-two.

It's a routine morning meeting in the Vatican, the kind where cardinals gather to approve dates for new saints. The business is done. Then the pope picks up a sheet of paper and begins to read, in Latin. Not everyone in the room follows the Latin at speed. Those who do go very still. He is saying that he has examined his conscience before God, again and again, and that his strength, with advancing age, is no longer enough for the work. And so he is renouncing the ministry of the bishop of Rome. On a set evening, at a set hour, the see of Peter will be empty. Then he puts the paper down.
screen: `A ROUTINE MEETING, IN LATIN.` → `MY STRENGTH IS NO LONGER ENOUGH.` → `THE SEE OF PETER WILL BE EMPTY.`

segments.voice: That morning raises four questions. First, was it allowed? Yes. People were stunned, but nothing in it broke the Church's law. The Church's law has a short line for this: a pope may renounce his office, provided he does it freely and makes it properly known, and it needs nobody's acceptance. Second, the reason he gave. He named no scandal and no pressure. He named his own body and mind. He said the work of a pope, in a fast-changing world, needs vigor of both, and that in him that vigor had declined. He didn't dress it up. Third, what came after. He did not go far. He moved into a small monastery inside the Vatican gardens, wore white, called himself pope emeritus, and said he would serve the Church hidden from the world, by prayer. Some theologians and canon lawyers have questioned parts of that arrangement, the title and the white, and they still discuss what a retired pope should be. Fourth, what it says. Ecclesiastes, in the Douay-Rheims, begins a poem: "All things have their season." A few lines on it says there is "a time to keep, and a time to cast away." Catholics read Benedict's choice in more than one way. Some saw courage and humility, a man putting the work above his own place in it. Some were unsettled, and wondered what it would mean for the papacy after him. Whichever way you read it, he did a hard thing plainly: he said, I can't do this well anymore, and he stepped down.
screen: `THE CHURCH'S LAW ALLOWS IT.` · `HONEST ABOUT BODY AND MIND.` · `A MONASTERY IN THE GARDENS.` · `ALL THINGS HAVE THEIR SEASON.` · then, large: `HE STEPPED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of something honestly. Settle, and breathe. Is there something you're holding on to because letting go would look like failure? A role, a commitment, a habit, a grudge, a title. Not everything should be dropped. Just ask the question Benedict asked himself: can I still do this well? Answer as plainly as he did, to yourself, without excuses or drama. If you pray, you can bring the answer to God. If you don't, just let it be true for a minute. The bell holds the time.
A resignation. Benedict the Sixteenth's renunciation, read in Latin to a gathering of cardinals, because his strength was no longer enough for the work.
Your line: he stepped down. Today, if your answer was no, take one small step toward handing that thing on, and tell someone you trust. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

933.title: Francis (2013–2025)
933.hook: a Jesuit from Buenos Aires takes the name of the poor man of Assisi
933.carry: a poor church for the poor
933.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the pope by name in the Eucharistic Prayer at every Mass; parishes take up Francis's emphasis through food pantries, prison ministry and visits to the sick and lonely.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a resignation: Benedict read his decision in Latin and stepped aside. Your line was he stepped down. Did you hand anything on? Today, the man elected after him. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

White smoke, a wet evening, a square full of umbrellas. A man in plain white steps onto the balcony of St Peter's and, for a moment, just stands there. Then he says good evening, like a neighbor. Before he gives the crowd his blessing, he asks them for something: to pray for him first, in silence. And he bows his head. The square, full a moment ago of noise, goes quiet. His name was Jorge Mario Bergoglio, a Jesuit and the archbishop of Buenos Aires. And the name he chose was Francis.
screen: `WHITE SMOKE, UMBRELLAS.` → `GOOD EVENING.` → `PRAY FOR ME FIRST.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. A few days later he told journalists how it happened. As the votes added up, a cardinal friend beside him hugged him and said, don't forget the poor. And the name came to him: Francis of Assisi, the man of poverty, the man of peace, who loved creation. You have met Francis of Assisi on this path before: the merchant's son who gave everything away. Second, the line. In that same talk he said how much he would like a Church that is poor, and for the poor. That became today's line. Third, the habits. He lived in a guesthouse instead of the papal apartment. On Holy Thursday he often went to a prison and washed the feet of prisoners, women and men, Catholics and others. He kept phoning ordinary people who had written to him. Small things, said deliberately. Fourth, the scripture under it all. Jesus's parable of the judgment, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Francis pointed to that chapter of Matthew more than once. He also had critics: some Catholics found his style loose or his words unclear, and argued with his decisions on marriage and the liturgy; others felt he hadn't gone far enough. Both arguments ran through his years as pope. But the first evening already held the picture: a man who bowed before he blessed the crowd, and asked a Church to stay close to the poor.
screen: `DON'T FORGET THE POOR.` · `A CHURCH POOR, AND FOR THE POOR.` · `A GUESTHOUSE, A PRISON, A PHONE CALL.` · `THE LEAST OF THESE.` · then, large: `YOU DID IT TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan something simple. Settle, and breathe. Francis's style was small, deliberate acts. So think of one simple thing within reach today. Learning the name of the person who sells you coffee. Calling someone who lives alone. Giving to someone who asks, and looking them in the eye. Pick one. Don't make it bigger than it is. Picture yourself doing it, and notice where you'd be tempted to skip it. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve. If you don't, just decide. The bell holds the time.
Francis. Jorge Mario Bergoglio, a Jesuit from Buenos Aires, who took the name of Francis of Assisi because a friend told him not to forget the poor.
Your line: a poor church for the poor. Today, do the simple thing you picked, and do it in person if you can. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

934.title: The Year of Mercy (2015–2016)
934.hook: a jubilee where Doors of Mercy opened in cathedrals around the world, not only in Rome
934.howItsDone: In a jubilee year Catholics make pilgrimage through a Holy Door, usually with confession, Communion and prayer for the pope's intentions; the works of mercy are taught in parishes and practiced through parish outreach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis, the Jesuit who took the name of the poor man of Assisi. Your line was a poor church for the poor. How did your simple thing go? Day nine hundred thirty-four.

A heavy door, usually sealed shut, swings open, and people start walking through it. Slowly, some touching the frame, some carrying children, some in wheelchairs pushed by friends. It's only a doorway. On the other side is the same church floor. But in a jubilee year, walking through a Holy Door is a pilgrimage in a few steps. The best-known Holy Doors are in Rome's great basilicas, and to walk through one of those you had to get there. Then Pope Francis called a jubilee and asked that doors like this be opened in cathedrals and shrines everywhere, so that people who could never travel to Rome could walk through one at home.
screen: `A SEALED DOOR SWINGS OPEN.` → `A PILGRIMAGE IN A FEW STEPS.` → `NOT ONLY IN ROME.`

segments.voice: The year rested on four things. First, the opening line. Francis announced the jubilee in a document named for its first words, Misericordiae vultus, the face of mercy. It begins by saying that Jesus Christ is the face of the Father's mercy. Second, the motto: merciful like the Father. It comes from Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Third, the door. Jesus says in John's Gospel, "I am the door. By me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved." The Holy Door is that line made into wood and hinges. The document asked that a Door of Mercy be opened in the cathedral of each diocese, and could also be opened at other churches and shrines. Walking through it, with confession and prayer, was a way of receiving the jubilee's grace, the indulgence. Fourth, the works. The document asked Catholics to rediscover the works of mercy. The corporal ones: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, welcome the stranger, heal the sick, visit the imprisoned, bury the dead. And the spiritual ones, among them: counsel the doubtful, comfort the afflicted, forgive offenses, bear wrongs patiently, pray for the living and the dead. Francis also sent out priests he called Missionaries of Mercy, to preach and to hear confessions. The door was the symbol; the works were the point. A door you walk through in a few seconds, and then a whole list of things to do on the other side.
screen: `THE FACE OF MERCY.` · `MERCIFUL LIKE THE FATHER.` · `I AM THE DOOR.` · `THE WORKS OF MERCY.` · then, large: `BE YE THEREFORE MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk through a church door as a prayer, or get ready to. Settle, and breathe. If there's a church near you, picture its door: the handle, the weight of it, the step down or up. If not, picture any doorway you pass through every day. Choose one work of mercy from the list, the one you'd most like to have done for you. Then imagine walking through that door carrying it. If you pray, you can say the line from John, I am the door. If you don't, just let the doorway mean something today. The bell holds the time.
Misericordiae vultus. The face of mercy, the document in which Pope Francis announced the Year of Mercy and asked that Holy Doors be opened in cathedrals everywhere.
Your line: the door of mercy. Today, every time you go through a door, let it remind you of the work of mercy you chose, and do it once. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

935.title: Human fraternity (2019)
935.hook: Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar sign a document on fraternity in Abu Dhabi
935.howItsDone: Catholic dioceses and parishes take part in interreligious dialogue with local mosques and Muslim communities, sharing meals, joint service projects and study, and some mark the International Day of Human Fraternity, set by the United Nations on the anniversary of the signing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Year of Mercy, called Misericordiae vultus, and Holy Doors opened in cathedrals far from Rome. Your line was the door of mercy. Which work of mercy did you carry through a doorway? Day nine hundred thirty-five.

Two men sit at a table in Abu Dhabi, each with a pen. One is the pope, in white. The other is Ahmad al-Tayyeb, the Grand Imam of al-Azhar, the mosque and university in Cairo, in his own robes and turban. Between them is a document neither of them could have signed alone. They sign it, stand, and embrace. It's called the Document on Human Fraternity for World Peace and Living Together. Its first words name neither Rome nor Cairo. They name God.
screen: `TWO PENS IN ABU DHABI.` → `THE POPE AND THE GRAND IMAM.` → `IN THE NAME OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Read it slowly and it moves in four steps. First, the opening. It speaks in the name of God, who created all human beings equal in rights, duties and dignity, and called them to live together as brothers and sisters. Then it keeps going, naming the people a phrase like that can skip over: the poor, orphans and widows, refugees, the victims of war, every human life that God forbids anyone to kill. Second, what it refuses. It says plainly that religions must never be used to incite war, hatred or violence, and that God does not need to be defended by anyone killing in his name. Two religious leaders saying that together carries a different weight from either saying it alone. Third, what it asks for. Dialogue as the path. Working together as the way of acting. Understanding each other as the method. These are not grand words; they're a job description for neighbors. Fourth, what it doesn't do. It doesn't merge two faiths, or pretend Catholics and Muslims believe the same things. You heard the line from Assisi a few days ago: together, not blended. Catholics hear in it the Gospel's own words, in the Douay-Rheims, where Jesus tells his followers: "one is your master; and all you are brethren." Muslims bring their own scripture and their own reasons. Both men signed in their own names, from their own traditions. And the two signers asked that it be studied in schools, universities and places of formation, so that the young would meet it close to home.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF GOD, ALL EQUAL.` · `NEVER IN GOD'S NAME, VIOLENCE.` · `DIALOGUE, COOPERATION, UNDERSTANDING.` · `EACH FROM HIS OWN TRADITION.` · then, large: `ALL YOU ARE BRETHREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to greet a Muslim neighbor. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a Muslim you know, or see often: a coworker, a shopkeeper, a parent at the school gate, a classmate. If no one comes to mind, think of any neighbor you've never really greeted. Picture saying hello properly, using their name, and waiting for the answer. A common Muslim greeting means peace be upon you, and you're welcome to say it if it's natural to you. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Human fraternity. The document signed in Abu Dhabi by Pope Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar: all people, brothers and sisters, and never violence in God's name.
Your line: brothers and sisters. Today, greet that neighbor by name, and ask one real question about their day. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

936.title: The empty square (2020)
936.hook: in the pandemic, Francis prays alone in the rain in St Peter's Square
936.carry: we are in the same boat
936.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass and in November especially, and the blessing Urbi et Orbi is usually given by the pope at Christmas and Easter, and on rare occasions like this one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, human fraternity: a pope and a Grand Imam signing one document in Abu Dhabi. Your line was brothers and sisters. Whose name did you use in a greeting? Day nine hundred thirty-six.

Evening. Rain on the stones. St Peter's Square, built to hold huge crowds, is completely empty. The city is locked down; a virus is moving through the world, and people are dying in hospitals without their families beside them. Up the wide steps, under a canopy, one figure in white walks slowly, alone. No crowd answers him. Cameras carry the picture into kitchens and living rooms and hospital break rooms around the world. The pope has come out to pray, for a world that can't come to him. And the reading he chose is about a boat in a storm.
screen: `RAIN, AND AN EMPTY SQUARE.` → `ONE FIGURE IN WHITE.` → `A BOAT IN A STORM.`

segments.voice: The service was plain, and each piece of it was chosen. First, the reading. Mark's Gospel tells of the disciples crossing the lake at night when a great storm comes up and the waves pour into the boat. Jesus is asleep in the stern on a cushion. They wake him, and in the Douay-Rheims they say: "Master, doth it not concern thee that we perish?" He calms the wind, and then asks them: "Why are you fearful? have you not faith yet?" Second, what Francis heard in it. In his homily he said the storm had shown that we are all in the same boat, fragile and disoriented, and all needing each other. The storm, he said, strips away the comfortable things we use to look secure. He didn't say the storm was a punishment. He said everyone was in it. Third, what stood beside him. A wooden crucifix from a church in Rome, which tradition says was once carried through the streets in a time of plague, stood out in the rain. And an icon of Mary from a Roman basilica. Fourth, the blessing. At the end he held up the Eucharist in a monstrance and gave the blessing the popes call to the city and to the world, over an empty square, to everyone watching wherever they were. Bells rang. Sirens could be heard in the distance. The picture is plain: a man alone in the rain, praying for people he would never meet, many of them dying alone.
screen: `THE STORM AND THE SLEEPING JESUS.` · `ALL IN THE SAME BOAT.` · `A CRUCIFIX AND AN ICON IN THE RAIN.` · `A BLESSING OVER AN EMPTY SQUARE.` · then, large: `WHY ARE YOU FEARFUL?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for those who died alone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who died in those months without a hand to hold. You may know some by name. If you do, let their names come one at a time. If not, think of a hospital corridor at night, a nurse holding up a phone so a family can say goodbye. Stay with them. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the nurses and doctors who stood in for families. If you don't, simply remember them. The bell holds the time.
Monstrance. The vessel in which Pope Francis held up the Eucharist to bless the city and the world, alone in the rain over an empty St Peter's Square.
Your line: we are in the same boat. Today, check in on someone who spent those months alone, and ask how they're doing now. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: Easter Monday, 2025
937.hook: Francis dies on Easter Monday, the day after blessing the crowd at Easter
937.howItsDone: Catholics keep the eight days from Easter Sunday as the octave of Easter, celebrating each day at Mass as Easter itself, and when a pope dies they pray for him at Masses offered for the repose of his soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the empty square, and the monstrance he held up: Francis praying alone in the rain, the great square in front of him without a single pilgrim. Your line was we are in the same boat. Who turned out to be in the boat with you? Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

Easter Sunday in Rome, and the square that stood empty in yesterday's story is packed. Flags, umbrellas, phones held high. On the balcony of Saint Peter's, a frail man in a wheelchair is brought out, his voice thin after a long illness. He wishes the crowd a happy Easter, and someone beside him reads his Easter message aloud, because he can't. Then, instead of going back inside to rest, he rides down into the square in the open car, slowly, through the people, blessing children held up to him. The next morning, Easter Monday, Pope Francis died. Today is about that day, and about where it falls.
screen: `A FULL SQUARE ON EASTER SUNDAY.` → `A FRAIL BLESSING FROM THE BALCONY.` → `THE NEXT MORNING, HE DIES.`

segments.voice: For some families, Easter Monday is a leftover day. In Italy it even has a nickname, Pasquetta, little Easter, a day for picnics and the last of the chocolate. But in the Church's calendar, Easter Monday is not simply the day after Easter. It is still Easter. The Church's norms for the liturgical year say that the first eight days of the Easter season make up the octave of Easter, and each one is celebrated as a solemnity of the Lord. At Mass that Monday, the alleluias are still ringing, and the prayers still speak of this day, as if the sun hasn't set on the empty tomb. Easter, the calendar says in effect, is too large for a single sunrise. So when the news came, Catholics heard it inside that long day. A man who had just blessed the city and the world on Easter died while the Church was still singing about the resurrection. One of the Gospel readings the Church offers for funerals is Jesus speaking to Martha in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me, although he be dead, shall live." The same promise is offered at the funeral of anyone who dies in the faith, famous or not. Francis seems to have wanted his own burial to look just as ordinary. He had asked to be buried simply, outside the Vatican, in the Roman basilica of Saint Mary Major, where he used to pray before and after his journeys, under a plain stone carrying only his name in Latin: Franciscus. For the world outside, Easter Monday is a holiday in some places and a workday in others. For the Church it is still Easter morning. Both were true that day, at the same time.
screen: `EASTER MONDAY IS STILL EASTER.` · `AN OCTAVE: EIGHT DAYS KEPT AS ONE.` · `A DEATH INSIDE THE EASTER SEASON.` · `A PLAIN STONE: FRANCISCUS.` · then, large: `I AM THE RESURRECTION AND THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the popes who have died. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the popes you've met in these lessons, or the ones from your own lifetime. Francis. Benedict. John Paul. Whoever comes. Don't sum them up or grade them. Just say each name slowly, one at a time, and let it rest. The Church's old prayer for the dead asks God to grant them eternal rest and to let perpetual light shine on them. If you pray, you can say that prayer after each name. If you don't, give each name one quiet breath before the next. The bell holds the time.
Easter Monday. The day after Easter Sunday, which the Church's calendar still keeps as Easter, inside the octave. The day Pope Francis died.

Your line: the day after easter. Today, notice one thing still going after its big moment has passed: a kindness from yesterday, a song still in your head, a meal still feeding someone. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

938.title: The conclave
938.hook: cardinals under eighty lock themselves in the Sistine Chapel and vote until white smoke
938.howItsDone: When the papacy is vacant, Catholics around the world pray at Mass for the cardinals in conclave, and crowds gather in Saint Peter's Square to watch the chimney for white smoke.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter Monday: a pope died while the Church was still singing Easter. Your line was the day after easter. What was still going for you after its big moment had passed? Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

The doors of the Sistine Chapel are about to close, and a voice calls out two Latin words: extra omnes. Everyone out. Staff, cameras, guards: out. Inside, under the painted ceiling, sit the cardinals who are allowed to vote. Their phones are gone. No newspapers, no television, no messages in or out. They will stay inside this closed world, praying and voting, until one name has enough votes to make a pope. Outside, a crowd in Saint Peter's Square keeps staring at a thin metal chimney on the chapel roof, waiting for it to smoke. Today's word is the name for that locked room.

segments.voice: Conclave. It names both the gathering and the locked-in way it works. The rules today come from a document John Paul the Second wrote on electing a pope, later adjusted by Benedict. Only cardinals under eighty may vote, and they swear to keep everything secret. The ballot is a card printed with the Latin for I elect as Supreme Pontiff, and a blank line. Each cardinal writes one name, in handwriting meant to be hard to recognize. Then, one at a time, he carries his folded card up to the altar, beneath the great painting of the Last Judgment, and says an oath aloud: he calls Christ the Lord, who will be his judge, to witness that he is voting for the one he believes, before God, should be chosen. It takes two-thirds of the votes to elect. After the counting, the ballots are burned in a stove. Black smoke means no one yet. White smoke, with the bells of Saint Peter's, means a pope. Then a cardinal steps onto the balcony and announces: habemus papam, we have a pope. The Church sees something old in this. In the Acts of the Apostles, before choosing someone to take the place of Judas, the apostles pray to the Lord who knows every heart and ask him to show which man he has chosen. Then they cast lots. The conclave keeps the prayer and trades the lots for ballots: human votes, counted carefully, held inside prayer. And this week's stories run straight through it. A pope who stepped down. A pope from Buenos Aires. A door of mercy, a signed brotherhood, an emptied square, an Easter Monday. Each of those popes walked out of this room.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one decision into a closed room. Settle, and breathe. Pick one choice in front of you, large or small. For the next two minutes, shut the doors on it. No phone, no polls, no checking what anyone else thinks. Just you and the choice. Hold up each option, one at a time, the way a cardinal carries his card to the altar, and notice which one you could carry up with a clear conscience. If you pray, you can ask, as the apostles did, to be shown the way. You don't have to decide yet. Black smoke is allowed. The bell holds the time.
Conclave. The locked gathering of cardinals that elects a pope, voting in the Sistine Chapel until one name has two-thirds of the votes.
Your line: white smoke. Today, when you finally settle something, even what to cook for dinner, notice the moment it's decided, and let it stay decided. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.
